column2: A questionnaire distributed to the community asks what each person thinks of combining academic work and physical work. Results: women students (1 indifferent, 2 unfavorable, 11 favorable, 15 very favorable); men students (2, 9, 11, 16); women teachers (1, 0, 6, 1); men teachers (3, 2, 6, 4). Full table of figures, courtesy of Forbes
Panofsky came to the college during the Alberses' sabbatical leave in 1941.

At the start of the 1941 academic year, after a semester at Harvard, Albers declares that he was not discouraged by comparing a 300-year-old institution with an 8-year-old one, since the younger, without much of a past, has remained alive and promising.

The college leaves the Blue Ridge buildings for the site of a former summer camp on the shore of Lake Eden, surrounded by woods, hills, and mountains. a former summer camp; a semirustic main building with a large social hall and a dining hall with a long screened porch overlooking the lake Consequences: a new setting for living and teaching

The college leaves the Blue Ridge campus (Lee Hall) for the site of a former summer camp on the shore of Lake Eden, several kilometers below. The site of a former summer camp surrounded by woods, hills, and mountains; a semirustic main building with a large social hall and a dining hall with a long screened porch overlooking the lake; a fieldstone fireplace. Consequences: New teaching possibilities tied to the surrounding nature.

Albers introduces the concept of matière by showing 28 magazine photographs with pronounced textures, with comments. A fashion photo: smooth skin and crumpled lace help each other; a whiskey advertisement: liquids, ice, and silver tickle the appetite; another: “Ice and roses. Cruel, but interesting.”

Albers presents 28 photographs of materials, including a fashion photo (smooth skin and crumpled lace) and two whiskey advertisements (liquid, ice, and silver; ice and roses). 28 photographs; “Ice and roses. Cruel, but interesting” Consequences: The matière exercise officially introduced into the design course

Writing in 1941, Albers specifies that these studies are technical exercises concerning only the craft of drawing, a necessary preparation for serious work; they do not directly produce works but develop discipline. The essential aim: “seeing eyes and obedient hands”.

Chaet, then a student in Boston, attends a lecture by Albers — his first encounter with him (dated 1941 according to Albers's inscription on a manuscript of the talk). Interviewed on January 5, 1996, by Fred Horowitz.
Photograph taken by Albers of the Studies Building under construction (ca. 1941).

At his death in 1941, Surette, founder of the Concord Summer School of Music, a member of the advisory council since 1933 and briefly a teacher, bequeaths to the college his entire library of recorded music. a huge library of recorded music Consequences: Feeds the musical saturation of the campus

Hired in the fall of 1941 as an apprentice teacher of the plastic arts, reclassified a year later in applied arts, then in 1943 put in charge of woodworking, a post she kept until her departure in 1947. Consequences: The building program intensifies, especially at the farm.
An exhibition of architectural models of low-cost houses, photographed by Claude Stoller; also a model of the four-wing Studies Building (dormitory, library, administration, classrooms).

In about a year, the students completed their individual work spaces in the 200-foot (about 61 m) building. The building: a foundation of local rubble stone, a wood frame, transite (asbestos) siding, International Style amid a rural Southern landscape Consequences: The building becomes an icon of the college and still stands today
Molly Gregory is hired as an apprentice teacher and the woodworking workshop is set up, where Kocher probably built his stool and table. Consequences: Woodworking develops at the college

A house designed by Kocher for the music teacher Heinrich Jalowetz; an experiment in acoustics with wall panels of perforated plywood and vermiculite ceiling plaster that visibly improved the sound of Jalowetz's piano. Claude Stoller was its job captain. Conventional and prefabricated elements; the house, slightly altered, is now a private residence Consequences: Stoller will become a professional architect

Young Mark Dreier, the child of the teacher Theodore Dreier, is tragically killed in a vehicle accident on campus; in his memory, Alex Reed (a student) and Molly Gregory (faculty) design and build the Quiet House, a simple one-room stone building. wooden doors painted white, black handles and hinges Consequences: A place of consolation, retreat, and renewal for this largely secular community

For Le Médecin malgré lui (1666) and Les Précieuses ridicules (1659), directed by Robert Wunsch, the student Frances Kuntz makes twenty-six costumes and the set on a 25-dollar budget: she sprays cheap muslin to imitate velvet, silk, and lace, and uses peanuts, shredded wheat, cotton batting, wood shavings, crepe paper, and mops to create elaborate wigs. a 25-dollar budget; 26 costumes Consequences: an example of visual ingenuity on slender resources

Wunsch produces the college's first literary magazine, “......toward a projected College magazine,” made up exclusively of student work, printed in the early 1940s as the United States enters the war. Four prose pieces and three poems; contributors: Jane Mayhall, Frances Goldman, Emil Willimotz, Robert Sunley, Sue Spayth Consequences: Creative writing begins to be valued as an artistic practice rather than an educational exercise
A document, “toward a projected College magazine,” dated around 1941, is preserved in the college archives; it supplies several notes in the article on the writing exercises.

According to his sister's recollection, at eight Rauschenberg had as pets, all at the same time, a horned lizard, a goat, a rooster, goldfish, and two hunting dogs that had a litter of nine puppies. a horned lizard, a goat, a rooster, goldfish, two hunting dogs, nine puppies Consequences: Alloway connects this menagerie with the stuffed animals of the combines (the angora goat, the eagle in Canyon, the roosters in Satellite and Odalisk).

In the summer when she is eleven, the boat bringing the family back to the island after a birthday party explodes. Susan is badly burned; her brother Danky, eighteen months older, dies. She remembers that she changed after Danky's death; their parents had labeled them — she the good one, he the smart one. the boat explosion; severe burns; brother and sister a year and a half apart Consequences: every year on Danky's birthday she makes a work for him; the family's first lasting contact with harsh reality; afterward the adoption of a girl and a boy; family life changed forever

An affectionate letter from the father (signed “Dad”): glad that Jean lets him ride her horse, he suggests that he may become a Pony Express rider; questions about baseball, the promise of a fielder's glove next time; he listens to the games on the radio almost every afternoon; he encloses a comic song about biblical baseball, in which Eve stole first, Adam stole second, Satan umpired the game, Rebecca took the pitcher to the well, Goliath was put out by David, Cain made a base hit, the Prodigal Son hit a home run, and Brother Noah handed out rain checks. A baseball glove, the radio, the song “Eve stole first”
Goodman writes a theoretical analysis of the frame and the screen, citing films and the state of the cinema in 1941 an explicit reference: still, in 1941, in the style of the 1925 Paris Exposition

In the midst of breaking with the political and moral values of American society, Goodman sets about revising a short novel composed in 1935 and finds that it is written in a manner he no longer commands: overdetermined symbolism and naturalistic detail have become intolerable to him. A novel composed in 1935, a revision attempted in 1941, an assessment made in 1945 Consequences: He draws from it a theory of the link between the author's psychological attitude and literary manner
A Black Mountain College meeting in New York; Albers declares himself opposed to the irresolute laissez-faire of many so-called progressive schools.
At the wedding of Frank and Ann Pace in Haverford, John Andrew and Nell Rice see each other for the last time. Consequences: The couple's separation ends in divorce.

As his divorce from Nell looms, Rice meets the woman who will become his second wife: a stunning blonde of Norwegian descent, a graduate of St. Olaf College, a secretary in Manhattan and a part-time singer in small ensembles. Consequences: Dikka will push Rice to finish his book; she will become Dikka Moen Rice.

In 1941, after she and her whole family have had to sell their jewelry or use it for bribes, Anni makes and exhibits necklaces of astonishing originality from paper clips, sink strainers, bobby pins, and other hardware and stationery items. Paper clips, sink strainers, bobby pins.

He builds the long room that serves as his studio, pours the concrete floor, and installs a row of north skylights tilted at 30 degrees; he produces about twenty sculptures a year there. skylights at 30°; two oil stoves; some twenty pieces a year Consequences: the “Terminal Iron Works” set up

Annoyed by the time Bill spends with Gorky, Elaine takes Gorky to another party to meet Agnes Magruder, nineteen, very beautiful and very elegant Consequences: Agnes becomes his second wife eight months later

An article on textile work at Black Mountain College published in The Weaver, vol. VI, no. 1, pp. 3-7. The Weaver, VI, 1, January-February 1941, pp. 3-7 Consequences: Makes BMC's weaving workshop known beyond the campus

While the truck driver runs his errands, Zoya explores and drinks at a fountain at the back of the store; she feels dozens of eyes boring into her back and turns around: everyone is staring at her. She looks for her mistake, then sees the sign: “For Colored”. Atmosphere: sudden unease, uncomprehending shame, a tipping point Stakes: the revelation of segregation; a decision to leave BMC a few days later

A few days after Asheville, while hoeing corn, she stops in the middle of the field, sets down her hoe, packs her bags, and goes back to Chicago to understand this country that saved her life and that denies freedom to part of its citizens. Atmosphere: a clean gesture, resolution in a sunlit field Stakes: a turning point in a life: a future civil rights activist

Back from a semester at Harvard, Albers compares a 300-year-old institution with an 8-year-old one and concludes that the younger, without much of a past behind it, has remained alive and promising. Words: He did not find the comparison discouraging. Atmosphere: The prickly pride of the small Southern college facing the northeastern giant. Stakes: Defending BMC's vitality against Harvard's respectability.

Albers shows 28 magazine photographs; he comments on a fashion photo (smooth skin against crumpled lace) and two whiskey advertisements (liquid, ice, and silver; ice and roses). Words: see how the two surfaces help each other, the smooth skin and the crumpled lace; “Ice and roses. Cruel, but interesting.” Atmosphere: A sharp eye turned on mass culture.

A young working girl buys herself an ice cream soda on her day off, then decides to buy a dress without trying it on; back home, the dress does not fit and her parents scold her for wasting her money Stakes: A lesson in modesty and thrift, imitating the moral stories of the PEA anthology

An old shopkeeper dissatisfied with his life of weighing nails and measuring rope sits on the wooden bench in front of his shop, looks at the dusty green station, and says he wants to create; the narrator wonders what he could possibly want to create Words: “I want to create,” says Mr. Goldfinch Atmosphere: The melancholy of unfulfilled creative desire Stakes: Innate creativity versus a life of work

On a gray day, the smell of pickles or mildew suddenly brings back a childhood memory; the adolescent sent by his parents to grocers they consider bad, sick, good-for-nothing discovers in them kind, hardworking people Words: “never again would I believe as I had in my mother, father, and all the adult world” Atmosphere: Sensory memory, smells, gray days Stakes: An allegory of the Black Mountain experience: leaving one's parents, thinking for oneself

Coming back from a birthday party toward Outer Island: the ferryboat explodes; Susan is badly burned, her brother dies. Atmosphere: a summer tragedy, a decisive turning point Stakes: the family's first lasting encounter with harsh reality; two children adopted afterward

On his round of former students in New York, Rice stops at the shared house on the Hudson; he leaves, the situation being too precarious for him. Words: According to David Way, he found their situation far too precarious; there were no rich people to bail him out. Atmosphere: Embarrassment, student poverty against the founder's need for comfort. Stakes: The social fall of the founder, now begging hospitality from his former students.

Albers writes that art cannot be analyzed to the end but that a clear head never hinders genuine feeling; he insists on exercises in movement, parallelism (horizontal, vertical, oblique), equality (repetition of signs), and spatial illusions; the aim: “seeing eyes and obedient hands”.

The new quarters are habitable, but barely: the interior of the Studies Building unfinished, the nine existing buildings to be insulated, the stone roundhouse to be turned into a music building, the bathhouses into chemistry laboratories, the cottages into faculty housing. 9 buildings to insulate Consequences: the move across the valley begins with the good weather

Day after day, the student Derek Bovington drives a tractor with an immense trailer between Lee Hall and Lake Eden: looms, pianos, books, kitchen and laboratory equipment, personal belongings — and the entire heating system of Lee Hall (radiators, pipes, bricks), to the dismay of the Blue Ridge Assembly. radiators, pipes, bricks carried off; a student will later comment “not terribly high-minded,” while arguing that the system belonged to the college, which had installed it at its own expense Consequences: strained relations with the Blue Ridge Assembly; Bovington will later die in the war
He leaves BMC after a year, money being short and the world calling. In retrospect (1977), he believes he learned there not skills but values: kindness, mutual respect, perfection in one's craft.

Students and teachers travel the country looking for money. Evarts, assigned to California, meets Henry Fonda (“a very good guy, he may even contribute a small amount”), the Fredric Marches (a very beautiful house, not too showy), Herman Mankiewicz (a sort of wise guy, but very cultivated and nobody's fool); only Melvyn Douglas actually gives Hollywood money. the only Hollywood money obtained: from Melvyn Douglas Consequences: funds so low at one point that all work threatened to stop

Just as everything was about to stop, Dreier announces that an anonymous gift of 5000 dollars has arrived in the mail; the regularity of these anonymous donors at the opportune moment will lead to suspicion that it is Dreier himself, alternating with a family contact or a Forbes. 5000 dollars, anonymous Consequences: the building work continues
Mary M. Atwater publishes in The Weaver (July-August 1941) a skeptical article titled “It's Pretty—But Is It Art?”, critical of Anni Albers's work. The Weaver 6, no. 3, pp. 13-14

The start of term is postponed two weeks to make up for the delay on the building site; almost all the students come back early to help. The college officially opens its new doors at the end of September, in half-finished buildings; on cool fall mornings, people eat breakfast huddled in coats. At the first general meeting, Albers, back from a year of teaching at Harvard, gives a speech on the pride of having only eight years of existence against three centuries of tradition. a 2-week delay; breakfasts in coats Consequences: a new era for the college at Lake Eden

Back from a year at Harvard, Albers opens the first general meeting and gives a speech comparing Harvard's three centuries of tradition with the college's eight years, proclaiming his belief in conduct, expression, metaphor, and the manual type. Words: “We are finally on our own grounds” / “Life means change. Our aim is forward.” Atmosphere: exaltation, the joy of achievement Stakes: the consecration of the new site and of the educational creed

A cascade of obstacles (including the miscalculation of having oaks felled, kiln-dried, and sawn in Asheville, when buying oak flooring from the lumber dealer would have cost the same and been quicker); the college suspends the academic calendar and everyone climbs onto the roof. Richard Carpenter, a young biologist terrified of heights, nails all day long on the roof. flooring from felled oaks, then kiln-dried in Asheville; barely a year later, Carpenter dies of lung cancer at 31 Consequences: the frame completed; a fir tree set at the highest point, wine and food in celebration, good-natured speeches

After Pearl Harbor, the college, long cut off from politics, reacts at first with disbelief: the first radio brought to dinner since the Willkie campaign; five months after the start of the war, a student asks the faculty meeting to stop thinking of BMC as a world unto itself. The war drains men and money; survival depends on a government training program, but only two options (the Navy's V-1, the Air Force Enlisted Reserve Corps) seem feasible, and the college has never been accredited. programs: Navy V-1, Air Force Enlisted Reserve Corps; the problem of national, regional, or state accreditation Consequences: a search for a training mission in order to survive

To meet the self-imposed Christmas deadline, the college suspends classes; everyone climbs onto the roof; Carpenter, a young biologist terrified of heights who has just arrived, climbs up and nails all day. At the end, a small fir tree is hoisted to the highest point, wine and food are laid out, good-natured speeches. Atmosphere: everyday heroism, the exaltation of sacrifice, a celebration at the top Stakes: overcoming the obstacles to finish the roof before Christmas — a poignant foreshadowing: Carpenter will die of lung cancer a year later

For the first time since the Willkie campaign (1940), someone brings a radio to dinner; a student notes her astonishment. Atmosphere: the disbelief of a community that had deliberately cut itself off from the world Stakes: the outside world bursts into Lake Eden

The college writes to various colleges to obtain statements that they would treat Black Mountain students like those of accredited schools; Antioch, Swarthmore, Reed, and the University of North Carolina (under its president, Frank Graham) send affirmative letters. Consequences: Black Mountain obtains its quota in the V-1 and Enlisted Reserve Corps programs

The faculty, having already given its labor to build the site, decides to draw nothing beyond $10 a month per person until the college's survival seems assured; some turn down posts elsewhere, one of them at $10,000. $10/month per person; an offer refused at $10,000 Consequences: Drastic economies for survival

The college takes out a second mortgage of $18,000 (on the first, $11,500 remains to be paid); a new fund drive in the summer of 1942 on which Albers, Kocher, Mangold, and Dreier spend almost their whole summer, while the rest of the community canvasses friends and neighbors part-time. $18,000 + a balance of $11,500; close to the maximum that could be borrowed Consequences: Precarious survival

Deprived of their specialist, who has been drafted, the staff builds the chickens a rather dubious shack; the chickens prefer the trees to the henhouse, lay very little, and end up eaten by the college. Consequences: An amusing failure of self-sufficiency

Fritz Hansgirg, a refugee chemist, and his wife arrive for the fall term of 1942 in a cream-colored Cadillac, followed by a Hammond Grand organ (installed in the dining hall for community use) and a dazzling collection of classical records. A cream-colored Cadillac; a Hammond Grand; classical records Consequences: Evenings of Bach and cookies that enchant some and horrify the “anti-Gemütlichkeit” element

Hansgirg and Straus inspect a large hole, 15 feet by 10, in the pasture, the remains, according to Hansgirg, of a thirty-year-old gold dig; large pieces of apparently pure mica lie around it; the government needs mica as an insulator, Soviet and Indian supplies being disrupted. A hole 15 x 10 feet Consequences: Hansgirg proposes an experimental mining operation; the faculty meeting breaks up with eighteen people building castles in the air

In two days, 250 pounds of mica are collected; the Colonial Mica Corporation of Asheville (a government agency) sends inspectors who judge the samples “good muscovite”; a full-time miner is hired to sink a shaft on the vein and galleries below. 250 pounds; “good muscovite” Consequences: Mounting euphoria

The Cohens, Germans who spent ten years in English-speaking countries (mainly Dartington Hall), and Bentley, 25, join the faculty Consequences: Forms with de Graaff, and later Foreman, the group suspected of collectivism

The Board of Fellows telegraphs the governor of North Carolina to protest the death sentence of William Wellman, a Black man convicted on flimsy evidence of assaulting a 67-year-old white woman The telegram's words: his death would be an unpardonable tragedy and a blow to the cause for which the nation is fighting Consequences: No effect, except to strengthen the college's reputation as a refuge for “nigger-lovers”

Sam Brown, the student Moderator, organizes a meeting on the teaching and learning process, but receives no response from the students. Brown makes remarks on education twice without eliciting any reaction Consequences: Brown identifies a growing gap between the students of the 1930s and those of the mid-1940s, less interested in educational theory

The North Carolina Conference refuses the right to grant degrees: a library with too few books, a guaranteed annual income and a faculty salary scale below the required minimums. Consequences: A search for accreditation through other universities (Northwestern, Chicago, Swarthmore, Johns Hopkins, Antioch, UNC, Bard, Stanford, Reed), May-July 1942

BMC is refused the right to grant degrees: a library with too few books, an insufficient guaranteed annual income, a faculty salary scale below the required minimum. Reported in a letter from Wunsch to W. B. Alexander (president of Antioch), May 7, 1942 Consequences: Accreditation approaches to many universities

The college estimates that its office and kitchen staff earn 30 to 50% less than elsewhere; two experienced secretaries and a bookkeeper receive only $30 a month plus room and board. $30/month, 30 to 50% below the market

Elaine briefly holds a full-time job at Liquidometer, painting the dials of aircraft instruments for the war effort, alongside Jackson Pollock; she shares her sandwiches, so that he ends up bringing two Pollock brought sandwiches, then two; “they were good”

During the summer of 1942 at Harvard, Albers conceives his Graphic Tectonic suite, zinc lithographs that manipulate the line to create space and symbolism, as in To Monte Alban. Zinc lithograph; Graphic Tectonic: Ascension (1942), 17¾ x 8½ in.

The family is interned with thousands of Japanese and Japanese Americans: first at the Santa Anita racetrack, then at the Rohwer War Relocation Center in Arkansas. Asawa refuses the status of victim, takes part in community life, and meets artists there informally.

When Bliss and most of the students and some of the male teachers leave for the war in 1942, Gregory takes charge of the woodworking shop, which becomes the heart of the building program; she also runs the farm and its accounts and directs several summer work camps in 1945-1946. making benches, tables, chairs, desks, chests of drawers for the workrooms of the Studies Building; the large classroom table and the benches of the Quiet House Consequences: Summer 1947: she raises the roof of the farmhouse to house two new families, then leaves a few weeks later; it takes two couples to replace her.

Mark Dreier, the young son of Theodore and Barbara Dreier, had died tragically on campus the year before; Alex Reed builds a memorial house with campus stone, a sacred and contemplative space, furnished with wooden benches designed by Reed and Molly Gregory. Rauschenberg will later photograph its interior light. Stone gathered on campus, integration with the original rustic cabins Consequences: A memorial monument at the heart of the campus

At the college Kocher builds a stool and a side table in maple, simple crossed structures: two interlocking boards for the base, a third for the round seat or the rectangular top. Maple, standard utilitarian forms slightly varied Consequences: Emblems of his warm, inexpensive modern design

Regensteiner comes to study weaving with Albers during the summer of 1942; she will later found the weaving department of the School of the Art Institute of Chicago Consequences: BMC weaving radiates to Chicago
Hayes is jailed and beaten after protesting when his wife and daughter are asked to leave the whites-only section of a shoe store
In the early 1940s, creative writing exercises appear for the first time in the senior division examinations, which mark the student's passage… (text cut off).

In 1942, the Asawa family is forcibly moved to an internment camp for Japanese; the family farm is confiscated and Ruth's father is separated from the rest of the family. After a loyalty questionnaire and the guarantee of a sponsor, Ruth is allowed to leave for the Midwest. The farm confiscated; a questionnaire on loyalty to the U.S. government; a sponsor required; a camp in Arkansas; a War Relocation Authority identity card (1942-1946) with a photo of Asawa, stiff against a black background, hair tied back, expressionless. Consequences: Asawa enrolls at Milwaukee State Teachers' College to become a teacher.

A high-school student imprisoned in a Japanese American internment camp during the Second World War, she begins making art there. Consequences: A prelude to her three formative years at Black Mountain College.
Wildenhain has her house built with Gordon Herr; it is a one-room cabin. a cabin of 12 by 20 feet; two rooms added in 1948; she lives there until her death in 1985

Stoller leaves BMC after the fall term of 1942, drafted into the U.S. Army. He had applied to the Enlisted Reserve so as to finish his studies and was turned down because he was deaf in one ear. deafness in one ear Consequences: He leaves BMC without a degree.

Graduates from Jefferson High School; enrolls in pharmacy at the University of Texas in the fall and is expelled after six months for refusing to dissect a frog in anatomy class. He was an ace at getting bad grades, he says

Glad to leave Port Arthur and its oppressive conformity, he enrolls in pre-pharmacy during the war years; painful studies because of undiagnosed dyslexia refuses to dissect a frog, a prerequisite of the program Consequences: this course of study fails

In the spring of 1942, Anni connects the jewelry with the war and with Mexican archaeological digs: many cannot go off to the munitions factory, but the need to act is growing; freeing oneself from nonspiritual values is the right direction.
Covarrubias, one of the first collectors to note the importance of the Tlatilco finds, carries out preliminary scientific excavations.

Goodman draws up the initial plan of this small study of his own writing methods. A plan dated 1942, taken up and commented on in 1945. Consequences: In 1945 he rereads his analysis as a schematic naturalism applied to his own work, a defense against it.

While writing a play, Goodman understands what always draws him back to the theater: the glorification of simple, manifest acts, the finite physical reality of a few actors on a small stage. Consequences: Defines the dramatic manner as a celebration of natural existence without any display of the author's power.

The writer and critic Malcolm Cowley comments that Rice's story as an educator brings to mind a train traveling through the night with its curtains drawn, ending its run at what should have been only a way station. The image of the train with drawn curtains.

Harper and Brothers names the book a winner of its 125th-anniversary prize for the best nonfiction work submitted before May 1, 1942; Rice shares the honor with the French émigré Julian Green (Memories of Happy Days). A $12,500 prize, shared; each share was worth about five times the average per capita income that year. Consequences: The money makes possible the move to Sarasota in the spring of 1943.

De Kooning refuses to appear in an exhibition organized by Peggy Guggenheim alongside Pollock, judging that he, like most of the artists shown, is too much under the influence of Surrealism. Consequences: He will accept in 1944 at Sidney Janis's.

Graham mounts a group exhibition mixing Americans (de Kooning among them) and established Europeans (Braque, Picasso, Rouault); it is there that de Kooning, who calls Graham his discoverer, meets Jackson Pollock for the first time. Consequences: The first meeting of two major figures of Abstract Expressionism.
Takes part in the exhibition “American and French Paintings” organized by John Graham for McMillen, Inc.; meets Marcel Duchamp and Jackson Pollock.

A small group exhibition of French and American painters, mounted by John Graham at the request of the gallery's owner; the critics receive it favorably, but no one buys the American paintings. No one bought American painting then; de Kooning sees a work by Pollock there for the first time. Consequences: De Kooning then gets to know Pollock.

Chosen by John Graham for “American and French Paintings” with de Chirico, Davis, Graham, Matisse, Picasso; meets Pollock and Duchamp; in March, “Artists in Exile” at Pierre Matisse's; Peggy Guggenheim opens Art of This Century at 30 West 57th Street.

The two men, each feeling overqualified, come upon a large hole in the pasture; Hansgirg sees in it an old gold dig thirty years old; large pieces of apparently pure mica lie on the ground; he immediately grasps their wartime value; he reports the find to the faculty and proposes a mining operation built into the work program Words: Hansgirg: they must dig to see what they can find; the elated secretary records the meeting as closing with “eighteen people building castles in the air” Atmosphere: Collective euphoria, a dream of financial rescue Stakes: The college's survival seems to hang on a hole in a pasture

For the fall term, the Hansgirgs turn up in a cream-colored Cadillac, followed by a Hammond Grand organ, generously installed in the dining hall for all, and a dazzling collection of classical records Atmosphere: The contrast between the refugee's luxury and the college at $10 a month Stakes: The arrival of a scientist interned as an enemy alien, whom the college accepts after a political check

In pre-pharmacy, dissecting a frog is required, a prerequisite of the program; he refuses Stakes: The young man's incompatibility with the curriculum, between moral refusal and the invisible obstacles of dyslexia

A lunch of watery hash and rice at school; Dawson feels strange when he meets his mother; in the car on the way to the veterans' hospital she lets him smoke a cigarette, but he does not feel well; the acrid smell of the hospital; his father is in the first bed on the left; he shakes his son's hand, then, with a wink, signals him to wait: he is listening to the game on an earphone and calls the plays as they happen — Creepy Crespi, the Cardinals' shortstop, runs behind second base toward right field, snags the hard grounder, somersaults, and, feet in the air, throws to first for the out; his right side paralyzed from head to foot, his right temple swollen by the tumor, the doctors constantly cutting away the growth, hideous red scars, his face askew; he holds his son's hand with his left; they talk about school and baseball, but he tires; the mother talks in a tender, superficial way, with an inner tone the child does not understand and that makes him angry and anxious; then the crisis: watering eyes, trembling hands, salivation, his stomach heaves; he vomits through his nose and mouth, over his shirt, his hands, his shorts, his shoes, and the floor, coughing, choking, crying; the father struggles helplessly to reach him; an orderly half carries him to a cot in the next room; his mother washes his face, hands, and legs; he rests and asks for a glass of water — his throat on fire —; barely back at the bedside, new convulsions, the water turns sour and comes back up mixed with bits of food; he drools, coughs, and cries while his mother, very worried, holds him. Watery hash and rice; the earset; Creepy Crespi's somersault; a cot; a glass of water Consequences: A founding trauma; an echo in the young veteran's wanderings

After watery hash at noon and a cigarette allowed in the car, the child walks up the acrid-smelling corridors; the father, an earphone in his ear, describes Creepy Crespi's defensive somersault; then the conversation runs out, the mother's tone angers the child; the nausea rises, vomiting through the nose and mouth, onto his clothes and the floor; the father struggles helplessly; a cot, water, a second crisis; his mother holds him. Words: The father calls the game live, asking with a wink for him to wait Atmosphere: The smell of the hospital, bodily terror, the helplessness of the two males Stakes: The author's founding trauma, material for a flashback
Photograph of Josef Albers drawing a lily for his class, taken by Tom Leonard in April 1942. Subject of the drawing: a lily; photographer: Tom Leonard
Josef Albers draws a lily before his students while Tom Leonard takes a photograph. Stakes: A living illustration of Albers's method of observation: showing by drawing, opening the eyes.
